key: Showcase: Darlene Naponse – Witness: Arctic Indigenous Voices
about: What does it mean to make films that tell stories not about land but from within it? Taking as its departure point Indigenous Anishinaabe perspectives on land as a web of relationships – encompassing everything above, below and around us – this Forum event devotes itself to an exploration of Darlene Naponse’s pioneering practice of land-based filmmaking. By taking a close look at three of her early short works and excerpts from her feature film AKI (2025), we will trace her more than two decades of Indigenous community-based filmmaking. How does one’s land shape the conception, production and presentation of filmmaking, and what sort of understanding can emerge from this practice for our con

key: Fishbowl: Handling of AI in Documentary Films – To Whom Does Reality Belong?
about: When and how should AI-generated images or voices be labelled? Can AI avatars help to render protagonists anonymous in a responsible way? And how should festivals and curators approach AI-generated works? Particularly in the field of documentary film, the presence of generative AI raises new questions regarding authenticity and ethical responsibility. Under what circumstances can it be used in a reasonable or beneficial way? And when should it not be used at all? Generative AI opens up new narrative and creative possibilities and makes the act of filmmaking more accessible. At the same time, it threatens to alter existing professional fields fundamentally, or even to supplant them entirely.

key: Roundtables: Short Film Distribution and Sales
about: How does festival strategy work for short films? And how do international distribution and sales look in this field? This is your chance to ask all the questions you always wanted to ask. Filmmakers will be grouped together and rotate between tables focused on festival strategy, sales and acquisition. Experts at each table will respond to your questions and topics – open discussion and exchanging knowledge and tips among filmmakers is also explicitly encouraged.

key: In Conversation with Talal Afifi: What Can a Militant Image Do? Sudan, Political Cinema and the Conditions of Visibility
about: Militant cinema is often associated with the anti-colonial movements and liberation struggles of the 1960s and 1970s. However, the motivating factors behind the practice – war, occupation, authoritarianism and the fight to control images – are more prevalent than ever in our current moment. In conversation with Sudanese curator/producer Talal Afifi, we will explore what militant film can mean today – not as a genre or visual style, but as relationships between filmmakers and the communities with which they collaborate.Curated in co-operation with Sudan Film Factory.Taking place at Roter Salon at Volksbühne

key: Case Study: Passing Through a Cloud of Mist – Filming in Haiti with Wilmarc Val
about: Since 2019 – perhaps even since gaining independence in 1804 – Haiti has been in the midst of a deep political, social and structural crisis. At the same time, the desire to make films in Haiti seems stronger than ever among a new generation of filmmakers. Wilmarc Val, who left Haiti at the age of four and grew up in France, is one of them. His films take him back to his roots: to a country that he must become reacquainted with from an outsider perspective, to his family history and to questions of origin, faith and identity. Here, filmmaking becomes a form of return, despite – but also precisely because of – the uncertainty that continues to characterise Haiti to this day.

key: Workshop: Curating Films – Women in Revolution in West Asia
about: Accompanying and drawing on the FOCUS program Revolutionary Women of West Asia, which treats feminist and revolutionary perspectives in the region, this workshop provides a look at the entire curation process. How does a program take shape, and what conceptional decisions have to be made along the way? Step by step, we will follow the process, discuss key questions and speak about which knowledge, expertise and networks are essential for responsible curation. In addition, taking two films as examples, we will provide insight into the specific challenges involved in curatorial practice.

key: Case Study: Representation of Forced Displacement in Film
about: Large numbers of displaced people continue to risk their lives attempting to flee across the Mediterranean – although the route has grown more treacherous and deadly than ever. At the same time, the ongoing catastrophe has increasingly vanished from the media and public consciousness. This case study asks how cinema can break through our visual habits and fatigue without instrumentalising suffering. The panelists will speak about trauma, anonymity, power dynamics, and how the film industry can engage responsibly with experiences of forced displacement.

key: Case Study: Desire on Screen – Not Without Disability with Lotte Sweeney & Maiah Stewardson
about: When it comes to individuals with disabilities, depictions of desire still often perpetuate ableist images and stereotypes. Taking the Australian short film The Knight as an example of best practice, this case study demonstrates what discrimination-conscious collaboration with disabled actors can look like in concrete terms. Dance, improvisation, personal storytelling and intimacy coordination become tools for creating authentic, accessible processes – and for crafting stories in which sex, desire and identity are a natural part of the everyday realities of people with disabilities.
